title: Thomas More and Erasmus
hook: two friends, a book called Utopia, and humor with holiness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Juan Diego, carrying flowers in his cloak to a bishop who doubted him. Your line was the little one.

A scholar is riding on horseback, the long way back from Italy to England, with hours to fill. Rather than waste them, he starts composing a joke in his head: a whole book spoken by Folly herself, a lady who praises fools and mocks the wise. He's on his way to stay with a friend in London, and the friend's name gives him the title. The scholar is Erasmus. The friend is Thomas More.
screen: `A LONG RIDE FROM ITALY.` → `A BOOK SPOKEN BY FOLLY.` → `A FRIEND IN LONDON.`

segments.voice: Start with the pun. Erasmus wrote the book in Latin with a Greek title, Moriae Encomium, the Praise of Folly. In his letter to More at the front, he explains: moria is Greek for folly, and it sounds like More's name. His friend, he adds, is as far from folly as his name is close to it. A joke between friends, printed in a book. Erasmus once wrote a long letter describing More for someone who had never met him: a face that leans toward cheerfulness, a love of jokes from boyhood, a knack for finding something to enjoy in almost anyone, and at the same time a man serious about prayer and generous to the poor. Then, More's own book, Utopia. A traveler describes an island run differently: property shared, gold despised, worship tolerant. The name is a made-up word, and the book plays games with it. Readers still argue about how much More meant and how much was a joke with a sting in it. That uncertainty is part of the fun. Finally, holiness. More is a canonized saint, and the stories told about his last days say he kept joking to the end. Wit, for him, didn't compete with faith. In the Douay-Rheims, Ecclesiastes says there is "A time to weep, and a time to laugh." These two friends seem to have taken both halves of that line seriously.
screen: `MORIA, AND MORE.` · `A FACE THAT LEANS TOWARD CHEER.` · `AN ISLAND CALLED UTOPIA.` · `A SAINT WHO KEPT JOKING.` · then, large: `A TIME TO LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one friend you've laughed with until you couldn't stop: where you were, what set it off, their face. Let a smile come if it wants to. If you pray, give thanks for that friend by name; if you don't, just stay with the memory and let it warm the room.
Utopia. Thomas More's book about an island run differently, written while trading jokes in Latin with his friend Erasmus. Today's word.
Your line: witty and holy. Laughter and prayer can share the same life. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Thomas More, with Saint John Fisher, on a shared feast in June; he is the patron of statesmen and politicians, and some lawyers' guilds take his name.

chat.says: Is Utopia a serious plan for a perfect society?
options: Readers still argue; it mixes real ideas with jokes, and even its name is wordplay.
Yes. More wrote it as an exact plan he wanted England to follow.
No. Erasmus wrote it as a satire to mock his friend More's politics.

notes: Praise of Folly's dedicatory letter: composed on horseback while returning from Italy, the pun Moria/More, 'as far from folly as his name is close to it'. Paraphrased; confirm. The hook places the ride 'over the Alps, on his way to England' and the stay in More's London house; confirm.
Erasmus's letter to Ulrich von Hutten (1519): More's cheerful face, love of jokes from boyhood, devotion and generosity. Paraphrased; confirm.
Utopia: shared property, contempt for gold, religious toleration; the name's Greek wordplay is mentioned without giving an etymology. Confirm.
'The stories told about his last days say he kept joking to the end' (Roper's Life; the scaffold remark): attributed, not quoted.
Original: μωρία (folly); confirm accent and pronunciation.
howItsDone: shared feast of Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, June 22; More named patron of statesmen and politicians by John Paul II. Dates omitted.
